title: Thermochemistry and Thermodynamics
description: Heat, energy, disorder and the question of which reactions can happen.

entries.name: Internal energy and the first law
entries.tagline: Energy is never created or destroyed. It only moves around or changes form.

sections.text: Thermodynamics splits the world into the system, which is the part you are studying, and the surroundings, which is everything else. The internal energy U of the system is the total of the kinetic and potential energy of its particles.
The change in internal energy equals the heat q added to the system plus the work w done on it.

points: q is positive when heat flows into the system and negative when it flows out.
w is positive when the surroundings do work on the system (compression) and negative when the system does work (expansion).
For a gas expanding against constant pressure, w = −PΔV.

sections.text: A system absorbs 100 J of heat and does 40 J of work on its surroundings. ΔU = +100 + (−40) = +60 J.

quiz.q: A system absorbs 100 J of heat and does 40 J of work on its surroundings. What is ΔU?

entries.name: Enthalpy
entries.tagline: The heat of a reaction at constant pressure.

sections.text: Enthalpy, H, is defined as H = U + PV. Most lab reactions happen at constant pressure in an open container, and the heat exchanged then equals the enthalpy change ΔH.

points: ΔH is negative for an exothermic reaction and positive for an endothermic one. It is usually given in kJ per mole of reaction as written.
A thermochemical equation includes ΔH: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −572 kJ.
Reversing the equation changes the sign of ΔH.
Multiplying the equation by a number multiplies ΔH by the same number.
ΔH depends on the physical states, so they must be written.

sections.text: ΔH° with a degree sign means the reactants and products are in their standard states, usually the most stable form at 1 bar, and often quoted at 298 K.

quiz.q: If a reaction has ΔH = −200 kJ, the reverse reaction has ΔH equal to…

entries.name: Hess's law
entries.tagline: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same however you get there.

sections.text: Enthalpy is a state function, so the total change depends only on the starting and finishing substances, not on the route. That means you can add up the ΔH values of steps to get the ΔH of an overall reaction you cannot measure directly.

sections.h: Worked example: burning carbon to carbon monoxide
points: C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ
CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ
Reverse the second reaction so CO is on the right: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, ΔH = +283.0 kJ.
Add them: C + ½O₂ → CO, ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ.

sections.text: Reverse equations to put substances on the correct side, multiply them to match the coefficients, add them up so the unwanted substances cancel, and apply the same changes to ΔH.

quiz.q: Hess's law works because enthalpy is…

entries.name: Enthalpy of formation
entries.tagline: A reference table that lets you calculate the ΔH of almost any reaction.

sections.text: The standard enthalpy of formation, ΔH°f, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states. By definition it is zero for an element in its standard state, such as O₂(g) or C(graphite).

equations: ΔH°(reaction) = Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ m ΔH°f(reactants)

points: ΔH°f values in kJ/mol: CH₄ = −74.8, CO₂ = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8, O₂ = 0.
Reactants: −74.8 + 0 = −74.8 kJ.

entries.name: Bond enthalpies
entries.tagline: Estimating ΔH from the energy needed to break bonds and released when new ones form.

sections.text: The bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in the gas phase. Breaking bonds takes energy, and making bonds releases it.
Bond enthalpies in kJ/mol: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 431. Broken: 436 + 243 = 679. Formed: 2 × 431 = 862. ΔH ≈ 679 − 862 = −183 kJ.
The values are averages over many molecules, so the answer is only an estimate. Hess's law with enthalpies of formation is more accurate.

quiz.q: In the bond enthalpy method, ΔH is…
quiz.a: Energy to break bonds minus energy released forming bonds
wrong: Energy released forming bonds minus energy to break bonds
The sum of all bond enthalpies
The enthalpy of the strongest bond

entries.name: Heat capacity
entries.tagline: How much heat it takes to warm something up.

sections.text: The heat capacity of an object is the heat needed to raise its temperature by one degree. Specific heat capacity is that per gram, and molar heat capacity is that per mole.
Water has an unusually high specific heat, so it takes a lot of heat to warm it and it releases a lot when it cools. This is why oceans keep coastal climates mild and why water is a good coolant.

quiz.q: Which of these has the highest specific heat capacity?

entries.name: Entropy and the second law
entries.tagline: A measure of how spread out energy and matter are, and why things happen in one direction.

sections.text: Entropy, S, measures how many ways the energy and particles of a system can be arranged. More possible arrangements mean higher entropy. It is often described as disorder.
k is Boltzmann's constant and W is the number of microstates, the ways of arranging the particles.

points: A solid melts or a liquid boils.
A substance dissolves, or gases mix.
A reaction produces more moles of gas.
The temperature rises.
Second law: the total entropy of the universe increases in any spontaneous process.
Third law: a perfect crystal at absolute zero has zero entropy.
Entropy is given in J/(mol·K).

quiz.q: Which process has the biggest increase in entropy?

entries.name: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity
entries.tagline: One quantity that says whether a process can happen by itself.

sections.text: A process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure if ΔG is negative. It is at equilibrium if ΔG is zero.

points: Spontaneous does not mean fast. Diamond turning into graphite is spontaneous, but it takes geological time.
ΔG° and the equilibrium constant are linked: ΔG° = −RT ln K.
Example: ice melting has ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol and ΔS = +22.0 J/(mol·K). ΔG = 0 when T = 6010 ÷ 22.0 ≈ 273 K, the melting point.

quiz.q: What does a negative ΔG tell you?

entries.name: State functions
entries.tagline: Quantities that depend only on where a system is, not how it got there.

sections.text: A state function depends only on the current state of the system: its composition, temperature, pressure and so on. The change in a state function between two states is the same whatever path is taken.

facts: Internal energy U, enthalpy H, entropy S, Gibbs energy G, pressure, volume and temperature.
Heat q and work w. Their values depend on the path.

sections.text: Climbing a mountain: the change in height depends only on the start and finish. The distance you walked depends on the path.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a state function?
